On May 20, OpenAI announced that an internal model autonomously disproved Erdős's unit-distance conjecture (using informal/natural language reasoning). Specifically, there exists a positive real δ>0\delta>0δ>0, such that for unbounded nnn, there exist sets of nnn points in the Euclidean plane with at least n1+δn^{1+\delta}n1+δ unit distance pairs.

This result with exponent strictly greater than 1 has been formalized in Lean v4.30.0. The formalization has been verified on lean-eval, which uses Comparator.

My primary interest in completing this formalization is two-fold:

  1. Correctness. While I can verify that the proof properly applies results from the literature, I personally am not familiar with the proof of the Golod–Shafarevich theorem and other results from algebraic number theory. I appreciate that Lean allows me to have essentially 100% confidence that the proof of this result holds end-to-end.
  2. Demonstration of capability. I am very interested in tracking the current level of auto-formalization. This proof was completed using Codex from OpenAI, with one person (me) in the loop. (I am a mathematician by training, but I don't understand all of what was formalized.) It took approximately one month.

I would like to thank the Lean community, the Mathlib community, OpenAI, and the authors of the texts used during formalization.

The formalization (linked above, and which you can browse here) includes 1.2 million lines of code. It takes hours and at least 10 gigabytes (I think) of memory to verify.

Approximately 800,000 of those lines are in files that are actually imported by the final result (which you can see here or here).

I don't have an estimate of how many lines there are only in results that are used directly, but perhaps somewhere around 400,000.
Congrats! Do you plan to document your work process? The kind of tools you used on top of the LLM (if any), what role you played, etc.

The formalization of only the "novel" portion of OpenAI's result is somewhere between 10,000 and 40,000 lines. The remainder is entirely existing results from the literature, including the Golod–Shafarevich theorem and a lot of class field theory. I used the following literature for Hall–Petresco:

  • J. Petresco, "Sur les commutateurs",
  • Philip Hall, "The Edmonton Notes on Nilpotent Groups",
  • Michael Chapman and Ido Efrat, "Filtrations of free groups arising from the lower central series".

I used the following literature for class field theory and its prerequisites:

  • Steve Wright, "Notes on the Theory of Algebraic Numbers",
  • J. S. Milne, "Algebraic Number Theory",
  • J. S. Milne, "Class Field Theory".

In particular, most of Milne's "Class Field Theory" has been formalized. (Unfortunately, I stopped after Theorem I.1.1 was available in characteristic zero, so some "final" positive characteristic results are missing.)

I also used the following sources, and I believe their (partial) formalizations are included in the repository but not on the import path for the main theorem:

  • Ruth Rebekka Struik, "On Nilpotent Products of Cyclic Groups" and "On Nilpotent Products of Cyclic Groups. II",
  • Alexander Cant and Bettina Eick, "Polynomials describing the multiplication in finitely generated torsion-free nilpotent groups".

There have been some related formalizations:

  • Kim Morrison formalized the literal negation of Erdős's original conjecture, which was about n1+O(1/log⁡log⁡n)n^{1+O(1/\log \log n)}n1+O(1/loglogn) unit distance pairs. This follows a different "one page" proof, poasted on X by Levent Alpoge. That result is weaker and does not require class field towers.
  • Logical Intelligence (Aleph Prover) formalized OpenAI's proof conditional on two axioms: Golod–Shafarevich and Shafarevich’s rank-relation bound. That formalization was 33,000 lines of code.
  • Kim Morrison added these two results to the Lean AI formalization leaderboard as golod_shafarevich_inequality and shafarevich_relation_rank_bound.
  • The Lean AI formalization leaderboard reports that the Golod-Shafarevich inequality has been proven by @LorenzoLuccioli with Aristotle (Harmonic) and @GanjinZero with Seed Prover (ByteDance) within the last week. No solutions are reported for the Shafarevich relation-rank bound.

Do you know about formalization.yaml? https://github.com/mathlib-initiative/formalization.yaml . In the past my first two questions about projects of this form are usually "how long did it take and how much did it cost" (the former you answered; the latter is some kind of proxy for "how many tokens did you use"). But formalization.yaml asks some far more detailed questions. Some of us are hoping that formalization.yaml becomes some kind of standard for reporting what actually went into an autoformalization.

Independent of all that, I was going to ask questions about exactly what you have proved when it comes to class field theory, but given that you have given us access to the repo I think I will try reading that first.

Several further formalizations should be possible:

  • The Shafarevich relation-rank bound, as mentioned above, should now be formalizable.
  • Shortly after the unit-distance result was announced, Thomas F Bloom, Will Sawin, Carl Schildkraut, and Dmitrii Zhelezov proved that the sum-product conjecture is false for real numbers. This result was formalized by Formal Frontier Team members Matthew Ballard, Fabian Glöckle, Bhavik Mehta, and Adam Topaz, with support from others on the Formal Frontier Team conditional on one axiom: Martinet's asymptotically-good totally real towers. It should be possible to remove this axiom. (Martinet's result itself is in lean-eval as martinet_totally_real_towers.)

I have access to unlimited Codex, but I believe the usage is similar to (or at most twice) a $200/month ChatGPT Pro subscription. Codex was formalizing for approximately 75% of the clock time for a month. The main interaction pattern, which is also my main takeaway for the whole project, is that you can just ask Codex "/goal formalize this book/article in Lean" and it does a pretty good job if the prerequisites are already available. (It might take some clock time, though.)

Regarding how much of class field theory has been formalized: I think that it would be nice to produce an honest theorem-by-theorem list, but as a first approximation:
As mentioned before, Milne's "CFT" was the reference used. Codex estimates that 2/3 of the book has been formalized, and I "estimate" that it's possible to finish literally everything that is proven in that book without too much difficulty. (Note: Chebotarev density is stated, but not proven, in the book, so it is not included in my comment. Though I think that, too, is fine.)

For some more general comments on chapters: Chapter II (group cohomology) is covered well. Chapter IV (Brauer groups) is nearly done. Chaper VII (global proofs) includes Brauer-localization injectivity but doesn't have unconditional global existence in Section 9. Exercise A-11 was needed for something and is complete.
Chapter V (global CFT) isn't great, but Proposition V.5.2 (the global Artin-map construction) is proven. Chapter VI (L-series and density) is weak.

Some of the strongest completed results:

  • I.1.1 is proven in characteristic zero,
  • Tate's theorems II.3.10 and II.3.11,
  • The global Artin homomorphism V.5.2,
  • VII.5.1 proves, for every finite Galois extension, the idèle class "second inequality",
  • VII.7.1 proves injectivity of the global Brauer localization map.

The following are NOT proven unconditionally: V.5.3, V.5.5, VII.9.5. VIII.4.2 has been reduced to VII.8.1, which needs a CyclotomicCaseBridge still. The following are also not complete: Chebotarev, ray-class L-function results, Grunwald-Wang, global quadratic-form classification, several higher-reciprocity results. But again, I think that they're mostly all achievable with auto-formalization and just weeks of time.

In another thread, Kevin Buzzard said:

The work of Golod and Shafarevich needs the existence of the Hilbert class field (a consequence of global class field theory, although historically earlier and perhaps easier) and also the Poitou-Tate long exact sequence and global Tate duality (harder than class field theory, or perhaps equal to class field theory depending on what your definition of class field theory is).

My formalization does not include any Poitou-Tate. (I don't know what the other two formalizations of Golod-Shafarevich include, but I doubt they go that route either.)
We have a proof of Chebotarevs density theorem here (the Dirichlet version)

Boris Alexeev said:

My formalization does not include any Poitou-Tate. (I don't know what the other two formalizations of Golod-Shafarevich include, but I doubt they go that route either.)

I don't think there are any other formalizations of "Golod-Shafarevich". When people say this they usually mean the claim about infinite class field towers, which is a consequence of two different bounds for cohomology groups, one due to Golod (which has been formalized and which doesn't involve class field theory) and one due to Shafarevich (which does need class field theory but it seems that my earlier post was wrong and one can get away with less than the full Poitou-Tate long exact sequence). The long exact sequence is just a succinct way of summarising various local and global duality statements, so it might be the case that Poitou-Tate is "essentially done" or perhaps the relevant part of it is essentially done.
Congratulations @Boris Alexeev ! I think the Class Field Theory formalization is just as much of an achievement as anything else in this project!

The Golod-Shafaravich inequality in the FRO's lean-eval is just the group-theoretical assertion. To apply it to the class field tower problem, one indeed needs something like Poitou-Tate. There's a bit of a naming issue with this area. Some people (e.g. me) say "Golod-Shafaravich" for the purely group-theoretical result, and some people (e.g. Kevin) say "Golod-Shafaravich" just for the class field tower problem.

@Boris Alexeev -- the assertion we left as an axiom in the sum-product conjecture formalization is here. I'm sure you could close that off as well :) Edit: I see you already pointed that out above! Sorry.

This is an impressive achievement!

There is an obvious question: are we any closer to getting class field theory in Mathlib? I'm assuming the default answer is "no, not at all", but maybe I'm being too pessimistic?

@Boris Alexeev Congratulations with formalizing the proof end-to-end!
As Kevin mentioned in #AI authored projects > Erdős unit-distance counterexample, exponent above 1 @ 💬, I would love to see a formalization.yaml in your repo.

Timothy Chow said:

I'm assuming the default answer is "no, not at all", but maybe I'm being too pessimistic?

The answer is "no, not at all" because the mathlib maintainers would simply block AI-written code like this, meaning that the road to class field theory in mathlib is long. You can watch the local part of the theory slowly taking place and being manually PRed to mathlib here https://github.com/kbuzzard/ClassFieldTheory . The global story is far harder.

Actually, that's not so clear. Certainly low quality AI generated PRs will be closed. I'm curious if anyone has looked in detail at individual files here and come to any conclusions about how well they are written. (This is our first significant sample of GPT 5.6 authored Lean code, so I think this is very valuable to investigate.)

I'm curious if anyone has looked in detail at individual files here and come to any conclusions about how well they are written.

I am about to start doing this. I started by getting claude to audit the code and flag anything which wasn't a theorem/definition/proof. It flagged this code in ./src/original/Towers/ClassField/CohomologyOps/ShapiroCounit.lean:

import Towers.ClassField.Shifting.ShapiroNaturality
import Towers.ClassField.CohomologyOps.RestrictionCompatibility

open Lean Meta Elab Tactic

elab "apply_private_shapiro_coind_naturality" : tactic => do
  let env ← getEnv
  let some (n, _) := env.constants.toList.find? fun (n, _) =>
      n.toString.endsWith "coindIso_naturality"
    | throwError "private coindIso_naturality not found"
  let goal ← getMainGoal
  let goals ← goal.apply (← mkConstWithFreshMVarLevels n)
  replaceMainGoal goals

namespace Towers.CField.COps
[etc etc]

but was also convinced that this was not malicious.

Hi @Boris Alexeev , thanks for sharing this output. I don't have access to my laptop for the weekend so I cannot try. But is there any way to make the project build or, as you say, it would take hours? If this is the case, since I assume you run it on yours, can you make the cache public?

From the repo:

rw [show (12 : ℕ).factorization 2 = 2 by native_decide]   -- 12 = 2²·3, so v₂(12)=2
rw [show (12 : ℕ).factorization 3 = 1 by native_decide]   -- v₃(12)=1

But these are not used in the proof, they're used in an example. (off-topic: my 2nd year project students ran into this and [got claude to] fix it -- I think they taught norm_num how to do it or something).
Yes, remember this has run through comparator (in my lean-eval setup), so it would be very surprising e.g. a native_decide was actually used (transitively) by the final statement

Thanks for sharing your project, it is surely an impressive achievemt.

I've had a look at random file that I think I am qualified to audit, Towers.NumberTheory.Cyclotomic.ClassNumberOne, and I see things like

/-- A precise Lean statement of Wright's Theorem 72.  Wright cites this theorem
without proof; the predicate lets subsequent deductions use exactly that statement. -/
def MasleyMontgomeryStatement : Prop :=
  ∀ m : ℕ, 3 ≤ m →
    (CyclotomicClassNumber m ↔ m ∈ masleyMontgomeryConductors)

Now, this Prop is true (according to the docstring), so it would be very weird for a human to organize the work in this way. It's probably enough to forbid doing such things, but I recognize the behavior of LLMs in organizing large repositories. @Chris Birkbeck can confirm that this happened a lot in our first tries of formalizing Kummer criterion: you can think that this is not a serious problem, but it makes think very hard to understand from a human point of view if the LLM gets stuck: if you ask "where is the problem?" you see no sorry, and declarations that give you the impression everything is done, but if you unfold things you see the problem, sometimes after a lot of work. Of course you can ask the LLM to help, but in my experience with chatGPT 5.5 and Opus 4.7 (4.8 wasn't a thing 2 months ago) they try to "lie" and don't explain well their difficulties.

Naturally, the impressive thing here is that the LLM didn't need any help from humans, so maybe my argument is just irrelevant.

Concerning a possible integration into mathlib, there are things like

theorem cyclotomic_five_number :
    CyclotomicClassNumber 5 := by
  letI : NeZero (5 : ℕ) := ⟨by norm_num⟩
  letI : NeZero (5 : ℚ) := ⟨by norm_num⟩
  letI : IsCyclotomicExtension {5} ℚ (CyclotomicField 5 ℚ) :=
    CyclotomicField.isCyclotomicExtension 5 ℚ
  rw [CyclotomicClassNumber, NumberField.classNumber_eq_one_iff]
  exact @IsCyclotomicExtension.Rat.five_pid (CyclotomicField 5 ℚ)
    inferInstance inferInstance (CyclotomicField.isCyclotomicExtension 5 ℚ)

where the definition of CyclotomicClassNumber is

/-- Class number one for the canonical cyclotomic field of conductor `m`. -/
def CyclotomicClassNumber (m : ℕ) : Prop :=
  NumberField.classNumber (CyclotomicField m ℚ) = 1

Now, as it is noted, mathlib already knows that the ring of integers if the 5-th cyclotomic fields is principal and the proof is kind of ok, even if I would remove the @.

They also prove it for eleven (also 7 and other small numbers are done, I am not sure why) and the proof is not very good honestly: you can compare for example the same proof in flt-regular (I don't think the LLM copied the flt-regular proof, the strategy is the same, it's the mathematical normal one, but the polynomials are different. The real difference is that in this repo is a big proof, without reusable subersults). The style is also quite bad (lot of @ and really a lot of have), but maybe this is golfable (by an LLM).

Also,the same proof would work for 17 and 19, but it would be very big (gigantic for 19). I think it's interesting to note that the LLM stopped at the same number we stopped writing this by hand (it's possible that the reference it's following stopped at 13 and this is why it did not 17).
Also notable from the repo: There are three axioms formulated in ClassField/Shifting/TensorAcyclicity.lean in order to state Remark II.3.12 from Milne's "CFT".

Riccardo Brasca said:

Also,the same proof would work for 17 and 19, but it would be very big (gigantic for 19). I think it's interesting to note that the LLM stopped at the same number we stopped writing this by hand (it's possible that the reference it's following stopped at 13 and this is why it did not 17).

The source is Theorem 72 here.
Thanks. Do you know if it's proved somewhere in the repo?

Probably not. The formalization was most successful when the reference it used provides a detail proof of a given result (although the model did have some success in solving some exercises that were given without proof).

Would you be interested in having a complete formalization of that result?
Something I find amusing it's that it uses this somehow ugly style of using a lot of @. My ChatGPT 5.5 "prefers" to abuse (a := p) instead of abusing @ (that is also bad if not needed).

Boris Alexeev said:

Probably not. The formalization was most successful when the reference it used proved the result (although the model did have some success in solving some exercises that were given without proof).

Would you be interested in having a complete formalization of that result?

Not really, it's a super technical result about cyclotomic fields. If you are think about the fact that implies FLT (historically it was one of the main motivation) we now have the more general result using Bernoulli numbers (it doesn't give class number 1, but it gives regularity, a weaker but more common condition).

This is our first significant sample of GPT 5.6 authored Lean code

Is it? 5.6 was only out for preview yesterday, while the project has been going on for a month ...

If it was indeed authored by GPT 5.6 then I would be curious if Boris Alexeev has noticed any concrete differences between GPT 5.5 and 5.6 as far as Lean is concerned.

Another question: I see that the project run on Lean v4.30.0 and current Mathlib runs on v.4.32: do you have a vague estimate on the time/cost that it would entail to update it to the current Mathlib version (both concerning Lean upgrade, probably minor, and Mathlib bump)?

Kevin Buzzard said:

The answer is "no, not at all" because the mathlib maintainers would simply block AI-written code like this, meaning that the road to class field theory in mathlib is long.

Suppose there were some AI-generated code like this that wasn't Mathlib quality, but that you had personally inspected and had convinced yourself was correct. If you needed the result for your Fermat's Last Theorem project, would you allow yourself to use it? This is a genuine question because I can see arguments both ways.

It might depend on all sorts of things such as "was the result known in the 1980s". For example, we certainly need some Class Field Theory to prove FLT from scratch, and the autoformalization which is the topic of this thread contains a bunch of class field theory, but (a) class field theory has been known for over 100 years and so I am allowed to skip it (b) I'm trying to compile some of the relevant class field theory statements in this AI-generated repo and things are not going well. For example the file Towers/ClassField/HilbertSymbols/Nondegeneracy.lean which I am currently trying to compile has seven set_option maxHeartbeats 1000000 ins and one set_option maxHeartbeats 2000000 in. The file itself takes an extremely long time to compile. If I put this file in the FLT repo then I will have to face compiling this file several times a week. The code in this file is terrible, e.g. 

        [] [14832306.000000] ✅️ letI : IsMulCommutative Gal(LF.toIntermediateField/K) :=
              by
              change IsMulCommutative Gal(L.carrier/K)
              infer_instance ▶

says "first let's incorrectly define a proof using letI, then let's attempt to get typeclass inference to prove it, and let's simply not care that our botched approach takes 14 million heartbeats, let's just increase the timeout". Of course nobody is claiming that the code is good, and to be honest I am probably the first person to be reading the code, but I have been working on this on and off all day and I still haven't even managed to compile the proof of the first main inequality of global class field theory because lean times out without me noticing. So certainly this code is going nowhere near my repo. However if someone were to tidy it up and make an upstream repo and keep this upstream repo up to date with mathlib (all of which is easy to do with AI but of course will cost money and I certainly won't be spending my own money on maintaining such a project) then perhaps I would consider using this as a dependency once we've actually done the post-1980s bit of FLT and I actually care about class field theory. So really the answer is quite complicated. I think an even more complicated question would be "what if an AI formalizes some of the post 1980s stuff" and here I think I might be tempted to try and refactor it until it's good.

I think a good practice, when managing lean-writing AI agents, is to have the rule "you are not allowed to touch maxheartbeats." I have adopted this and other similar rules, and as a result I don't think you will find many badly compiling files among the 450k lines in my stochastic homogenization project (which takes 26 min to compile from mathlib on 8-cpu machine).

So I think it is certainly possible to get AI agents to write better code than what you are describing.

Right now what seems to be happening is that different individuals or groups are all independently interested in the question "let's see if we can get AI to formalize this piece of informal mathematics" and I suspect that different groups are learning different tips. 

[Elab.async] [4716982214.000000] ✅️ Lean.addDecl ▼
  [Kernel] [4716982132.000000] ✅️ typechecking declarations [Towers.CField.HSymbol.hilbert_symbol_artin]

That is the largest number I have ever seen the profiler print. This is for typechecking, not elaboration. This indicates that something has gone seriously wrong somewhere. I am sure that the AI did not intentionally create a proof which the kernel would struggle so much with, so right now perhaps one question is what exactly went wrong.

[Meta.synthInstance] [6754991.000000] ✅️ Mul Gal(↥LF.toIntermediateField/K) ▼
...
  [apply] [3803971.000000] ❌️ apply @DirectSum.GradeZero.commSemiring to CommSemiring Gal(↥LF.toIntermediateField/K) ▶

bit of a wild goose chase there. But in general I think profiling this proof isn't going to tell me why the kernel takes 4.7 billion mheartbeats to typecheck it, and I suspect that the FRO won't be interested unless someone can minimise. In any case I should think that this would be a serious problem for getting the code into mathlib or using it more generally; typically such problems like this in code are fixed before they make it to mathlib, and you can see why; the file is incredibly annoying to compile (this is one of many declarations in the file which are taking forever for the kernel to typecheck; indeed the last 12 declarations in the file all take longer to typecheck than any Lean 4declaration I have ever seen before).

Some of the exposition is quite convoluted. For example

/-- **Theorem VII.5.1.**  The second inequality and the two low-degree
idèle-class cohomology assertions for every finite Galois extension. -/
theorem ideleCohomologyClaims :
    IdeleCohomologyClaims.{u} := ...

where

/-- **Theorem VII.5.1, source statement.**  No cyclic, abelian, or solvable
hypothesis is imposed on `Gal(L/K)`. -/
def IdeleCohomologyClaims : Prop :=
  ∀ (K L : Type u) [Field K] [Field L] [NumberField K] [NumberField L]
    [Algebra K L] [FiniteDimensional K L] [IsGalois K L],
    Claims K L

where

/-- The three simultaneous conclusions of Theorem 5.1 for one actual
extension and its actual idèle-class representation. -/
def Claims
    (K L : Type u) [Field K] [Field L] [NumberField K] [NumberField L]
    [Algebra K L] [FiniteDimensional K L] [IsGalois K L] : Prop :=
  (Finite (IK K ⧸ normPrincipalSubgroup K L) ∧
      (normPrincipalSubgroup K L).index ∣ Module.finrank K L) ∧
    IsZero (groupCohomology.H1
      (ideleCohomologyRepresentation K L)) ∧
    (Finite (groupCohomology.H2
        (ideleCohomologyRepresentation K L)) ∧
      Nat.card (groupCohomology.H2
        (ideleCohomologyRepresentation K L)) ∣ Module.finrank K L)

I think that more idiomatic would simply be to prove all 5 statements individually (it makes the results much easier to use). Also it seems to me that IdeleCohomologyClaims and Claims are defeq.

The final claim of Claims is that some cohomology group has size dividing [L:K][L:K][L:K] (the "second inequality" -- the harder of the two inequalities if my understanding is correct). What is this cohomology group? Those who know class field theory already will know that it should be H2(Gal(L/K),AL×/L×).H^2(Gal(L/K),\mathbb{A}_L^\times/L^\times).H2(Gal(L/K),AL×​/L×). So ideleCohomologyRepresentation K L should be AL×/L×.\mathbb{A}_L^\times/L^\times.AL×​/L×. We have adeles in mathlib already, so at least it should be easy to state. Let's take a look.

/-- The actual idèle-class additive group and actual Galois action, with
`ℤ` replaced by its universe lift solely so that Mathlib can form ordinary
group cohomology when the number fields live in `Type u`. -/
noncomputable def ideleCohomologyRepresentation
    (K L : Type u) [Field K] [Field L] [NumberField K] [NumberField L]
    [Algebra K L] [FiniteDimensional K L] [IsGalois K L] :
    Rep (ULift.{u} ℤ) Gal(L/K) :=
  let A := CL K L
  let _ := additiveIntRepresentation A
  Rep.of (uliftIntRepresentation (G := Gal(L/K)) (M := A))

So it's Rep.of something. We have

/-- The same additive action, regarded as linear over the universe lift of
`ℤ`.  Scalar multiplication by `r : ULift ℤ` is multiplication by `r.down`,
so no arithmetic data is changed. -/
private def uliftIntRepresentation
    {G M : Type u} [Group G] [AddCommGroup M]
    [DistribMulAction G M] : Representation (ULift.{u} ℤ) G M where

(do we really not have this? Why are we suddenly using Type u anyway?) and this definition surely should have G and M explicit. So really the question is what CL is. 

private abbrev CL
    (K L : Type u) [Field K] [Field L] [NumberField K] [NumberField L]
    [Algebra K L] [FiniteDimensional K L] [IsGalois K L] :
    Rep ℤ Gal(L/K) :=
  classCokernelRepresentation (K := K) (L := L)

Wait what? This is back to being a Rep? So we make a Rep of Int, translate it back into a Representation and then back into a Rep this time of uLift.{u} Int. OK so what is classCokernelRepresentation?

/-- The literal idèle-class representation `C_L = I_L/Lˣ`, formed from
the concrete Galois action on idèles. -/
abbrev classCokernelRepresentation : Rep ℤ Gal(L/K) :=
  cokernel
    (concreteActionData (K := K) (L := L)).principalIdeleHom

Hmm. So what is concreteActionData.principalIdeleHom? Well,

/-- The canonical Galois action on number-field ideles, with its placewise
transport and continuity properties. -/
noncomputable def concreteActionData :
    IAData (K := K) (L := L) where
  placeAction := numberGaloisAction (K := K) (L := L)
  preserves_finite sigma P :=
    ⟨(finitePrimeAction (K := K) (L := L)).smul sigma P, rfl⟩
  preserves_infinite sigma v :=
    ⟨sigma • v, rfl⟩
  transport := numberPlaceTransport (K := K)
  continuous_transport := field_transport_continuous (K := K)
  action := idelesGaloisAction (K := K) (L := L)
  transport_principal := number_transport_principal (K := K)
  coordinate_formula := ideles_galois_action (K := K)
  continuous_action := ideles_galois_continuous (K := K)

and

/-- The canonical equivariant diagonal embedding `Lˣ → I_L`. -/
def IAData.principalIdeleHom
    (D : IAData (K := K) (L := L)) :
    Rep.ofAlgebraAutOnUnits K L ⟶ D.representation :=
  Rep.ofHom
    { toLinearMap :=
        (MonoidHom.toAdditive
          (principalIdele (RingOfIntegers L) L)).toIntLinearMap
      isIntertwining' := fun sigma => by
        ext x
        change principalIdele (RingOfIntegers L) L
            (Units.map sigma.toRingEquiv.toRingHom x.toMul) =
          D.action.smul sigma
            (principalIdele (RingOfIntegers L) L x.toMul)
        exact (D.smul_principalIdele sigma x.toMul).symm }

Finally we are back to mathlib: Rep.ofAlgebraAutOnUnits is L×.L^\times.L×. So all we need to do is to check that D.representation is AL×.\mathbb{A}_L^\times.AL×​.

/-- The integral Galois representation on the idele group supplied by
`IAData`. -/
def IAData.representation
    (D : IAData (K := K) (L := L)) : Rep ℤ Gal(L/K) := by
  letI := D.action
  exact Rep.ofMulDistribMulAction Gal(L/K)
    (IdeleGroup (RingOfIntegers L) L)

Oh boy, it goes on. We're making it from a MulDistribMulAction (this is the third time we have switched between Representation and Rep). And this IdeleGroup looks interesting -- hopefully it's the units of mathlib's AdeleRing. Oh, it isn't:

/-- The idele group, with the product of the infinite-place unit topology and
the finite restricted-product topology. -/
def IdeleGroup : Type _ := (InfiniteAdeleRing K)ˣ × FiniteIdeles R K

Wait -- what is FiniteIdeles??

/-- The finite idele group, with its restricted-product topology. -/
def FiniteIdeles : Type _ :=
  Πʳ v : HeightOneSpectrum R,
    [(v.adicCompletion K)ˣ, IdeleUnitSubgroup R K v]

Gaargh, we have finite adeles in mathlib, and I had imagined that finite ideles would just be the units, but the machine has made another definition as a restricted product. And, for completeness,

/-- The subgroup of units in a nonarchimedean completion which are integral
together with their inverses. -/
abbrev IdeleUnitSubgroup (v : HeightOneSpectrum R) :
    Subgroup (v.adicCompletion K)ˣ :=
  (Submonoid.ofClass (v.adicCompletionIntegers K)).units

This is a huge amount of work for stating something which we basically already have -- however, it proves it too, so you can't really argue with it...
